Projectile motion
One model, two components
Original project-authored reference | Version 1 | 25 September 2026
Selected for the initial Phase 2 subject. Educator review pending; not approved for learner rollout.
S1. What the model represents
A projectile is treated as a point moving after launch, under a constant downward gravitational
acceleration. This model assumes no air resistance, no wind, and the same ground height at launch and
landing. It applies only until first ground contact. It does not model bouncing, spin, drag or a powered
object. Use metres (m), seconds (s), velocity in metres per second (m/s), and acceleration in metres per
second squared (m/s^2).
S2. Separate the two directions
Choose x positive to the right and y positive upward, with the launch point at x = 0 and y = 0. Let vx0 be
the horizontal launch velocity, vy0 the upward launch velocity, and g a positive gravity magnitude. In this
model horizontal acceleration is zero, while vertical acceleration is -g. The two components share the
same elapsed time t, but gravity changes only the vertical component.
S3. Equations of motion
Horizontal position: x(t) = vx0 * t. Horizontal velocity: vx(t) = vx0. Vertical position: y(t) = vy0 * t - 0.5 * g *
t^2. Vertical velocity: vy(t) = vy0 - g * t. Speed is the magnitude of the velocity vector: sqrt(vx(t)^2 +
vy(t)^2). A velocity component can be zero while the object still has nonzero speed.
S4. Apex and landing
For an upward launch (vy0 > 0), the apex occurs at t = vy0 / g. At the apex vy = 0, vx = vx0, and
acceleration remains downward at -g. The maximum height is vy0^2 / (2 * g). Return to the original
ground height occurs at t = 2 * vy0 / g, and horizontal displacement then is vx0 times that flight duration.
These formulas do not describe unequal launch and landing heights. A launch with vy0 = 0 from level
ground has immediate ground contact in this point model.

Apply and interpret the model
Source version 1 | Worked example and boundaries
S5. Worked example
Take vx0 = 4 m/s, vy0 = 12 m/s and g = 10 m/s^2. At t = 1 s, x = 4 m, y = 7 m, vx = 4 m/s and vy = 2 m/s.
The apex time is 1.2 s, its height is 7.2 m, and its horizontal position is 4.8 m. At the apex the speed is 4
m/s, not zero. Landing occurs at t = 2.4 s with horizontal displacement 9.6 m. Just before landing the
vertical velocity is -12 m/s.
S6. Compare valid cases and non-examples
If only vx0 doubles, every horizontal displacement at the same time doubles, while apex time and
maximum height are unchanged. If g doubles with the same launch components, apex time, maximum
height and flight duration each halve. If vx0 = 0, the flight is vertical; both velocity components are zero at
its apex for an instant, although acceleration is still downward. A feather drifting in wind, a powered
drone, or a ball landing on a higher platform is outside the declared model.
S7. Interpret a diagram carefully
A trajectory shows positions, not a force along the path. A velocity arrow shows instantaneous direction
and speed on its stated display scale. An acceleration arrow points downward even at the apex. The
linked height-versus-time view represents the same state as the motion and component views. A
flat-looking trajectory can result from a display scale; read the values and units. Changing a simulation
control demonstrates a model response, not a learner achievement.
S8. Explain, check, and acknowledge limits
When explaining a prediction, identify the relevant component, state the equation and units, and check
that the time is between launch and first ground contact. Explain why a zero vertical velocity does not
usually mean zero total velocity. State when drag, wind, propulsion or different landing height would
invalidate this model. A correct number alone does not establish the quality of a written explanation or
whether help was received.
